claims.claim: The lawful basis for processing personal data under GDPR includes obtaining consent from the data subject concerned, as stated in Article 16(C0) and Article 6(a).
Processing is also lawful if it is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party, as per Article 6(b).
Additionally, processing is lawful if it is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject, as per Article 6(c).

The GDPR also requires that personal data be processed in a transparent manner, including providing information about the logic involved in automated decision-making, including profiling, as per Article 13(f).

Furthermore, the GDPR provides that personal data should be processed for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes, and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes, as per Article 5(b).

The GDPR also emphasizes the importance of data minimization, requiring that personal data be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which it is processed, as per Article 5(c).
Consent must be freely given, without a clear imbalance between the data subject and the controller, as stated in.
Consent must be informed, with the data subject being aware of the processing of their personal data, as stated in.
The request for consent must be presented in a clear and intelligible manner, using plain language, and must be distinguishable from other matters, as stated in.
Consent can be withdrawn at any time, without affecting the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal, as stated in.

The right to withdraw consent is a fundamental right, and controllers must make reasonable efforts to verify that consent is given or authorized by the holder of parental responsibility over a child under 16, as stated in.
Prior to giving consent, the data subject should be informed of the processing of their personal data, and it should be as easy to withdraw as to give consent, as stated in.
A child must be at least 16 years old to give consent to an online service without a parent, as stated in Article 8 of the GDPR.

The GDPR requires controllers to make reasonable efforts to verify that consent is given or authorized by the holder of parental responsibility over the child, taking into consideration available technology.
Consent is presumed not to be freely given if it does not allow separate consent to be given to different personal data processing operations, as stated in Article 16 (part 56) of the GDPR.
The GDPR requires controllers to provide information to data subjects in a concise, transparent, intelligible, and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language, particularly for children.

The GDPR defines "processing" as any operation or set of operations performed on personal data, including collection, recording, organization, storage, adaptation, alteration, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination, or otherwise making available, alignment, or combination.
The GDPR emphasizes the importance of facilitating the exercise of data subject rights, including the right to consent, under Articles 15 to 22.

The GDPR allows for the processing of personal data for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes, as long as appropriate safeguards are in place.
Biometric health data can be processed without explicit consent if it is necessary for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes.
The GDPR requires that processing of personal data for these purposes should ensure the principle of data minimization.

The GDPR also requires that the further processing of personal data for these purposes should be carried out when the controller has assessed the feasibility to fulfill those purposes by processing data which do not permit or no longer permit the identification of data subjects.

The GDPR does not explicitly address the processing of biometric health data without explicit consent, but it does require that controllers provide clear and transparent information to data subjects about the processing of their personal data.
The GDPR requires that controllers provide data subjects with the right to withdraw consent at any time, without affecting the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal.

The GDPR does not provide a clear answer on whether processing biometric health data without explicit consent is lawful, but it does require that controllers ensure that processing is necessary for a specific purpose and that the data subject is not obliged to provide the personal data.

Data subjects have the right to erasure of their personal data, except where it is necessary for exercising the right of freedom of expression and information, or for compliance with a legal obligation.

The right to erasure also applies to personal data that have been made public by the controller, and the controller must inform other controllers that process such personal data to erase any links to, or copies or replications of, those personal data.

Personal data may be stored for longer periods insofar as the data will be processed solely for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes, subject to implementation of appropriate technical and organisational measures.
The right to erasure does not apply to processing that is necessary for exercising the right of freedom of expression and information.

In cases where providing information proves impossible or would involve a disproportionate effort, the controller shall take appropriate measures to protect the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests.
The right to erasure is also subject to the conditions and safeguards referred to in Article 89(1), which may limit the right in certain circumstances.

When personal data was not obtained from the data subject, the controller must provide the data subject with information on the identity and contact details of the controller and, where applicable, the controller's representative.
The controller must also provide the contact details of the data protection officer, if applicable.
The purposes for which the personal data will be processed must be provided to the data subject.
The categories of personal data concerned must be disclosed to the data subject.
If the personal data was obtained from a third party, the controller must inform the data subject about the recipients or categories of recipients of the personal data.
In cases where the origin of the personal data cannot be provided, general information should be provided to the data subject.
The controller must provide the data subject with direct access to their personal data, where possible, through a secure system.
The data subject has the right to receive their personal data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format, and to transmit it to another controller without hindrance.

The controller must be able to demonstrate compliance with the obligations under the GDPR, including providing information to the data subject, and be held accountable for the processing of personal data.

The controller should not refuse to provide all information to the data subject, but may request that the data subject specify the information or processing activities to which the request relates, especially for large quantities of information.

The controller and joint controllers must determine their respective responsibilities for compliance with the GDPR obligations, including providing information to the data subject, and establish an arrangement to reflect their roles and relationships.

The essence of the arrangement between joint controllers must be made available to the data subject, and they may exercise their rights under the GDPR in respect of and against each of the controllers.
A controller must respond to a data subject request within a reasonable timeframe, but the specific response time is not specified in the GDPR.
The GDPR allows a controller to charge a fee for providing a copy of personal data, but only if the request is "manifestly unfounded or excessive".
The GDPR requires a controller to provide information and take actions requested by a data subject within a reasonable timeframe, but does not specify a maximum response time.
A controller may charge a reasonable fee for providing a copy of personal data if the request is "manifestly unfounded or excessive".
The GDPR requires a controller to provide information and take actions requested by a data subject, including providing a copy of personal data, within a reasonable timeframe.
The GDPR allows a controller to charge a reasonable fee for providing a copy of personal data if the request is made by electronic means, unless the data subject requests otherwise.
The right to data portability requires that personal data be provided in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format, as per Article 20.
The data subject has the right to have their personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible, as per Article 20.

The exercise of the right to data portability must be without prejudice to Article 17, and the right shall not apply to processing necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller, as per Article 20.

The data subject has the right to be informed about the storage periods and applicable safeguards taking into account the nature, scope, and purposes of the processing or categories of processing, as per Article 23.
The data subject has the right to be informed about the risks to their rights and freedoms of data subjects, as per Article 23.

The data subject has the right to be informed about the right of data subjects to be informed about the restriction, unless that may be prejudicial to the purpose of the restriction, as per Article 23.
Automated decision-making and profiling based on special categories of personal data should be allowed only under specific conditions, as stated in Article 16 of the GDPR.

The existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, must be disclosed to the data subject, along with meaningful information about the logic involved and the significance and envisaged consequences of such processing.
Data subjects have the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, as stated in Article 47(f) of the GDPR.
Profiling is subject to the rules of the GDPR governing the processing of personal data, including the legal grounds for processing and data protection principles.

The GDPR requires controllers and processors to be transparent about their use of profiling and to provide data subjects with information on the logic involved and the significance and envisaged consequences of such processing.

The GDPR also provides data subjects with the right to lodge a complaint with the competent supervisory authority and to obtain redress and, where appropriate, compensation for a breach of the binding corporate rules.
The contract must specify the subject-matter and duration of the processing, as well as the nature and purposes of the processing.
The contract must set out the type of personal data and categories of data subjects, taking into account the specific tasks and responsibilities of the processor.
The contract must provide sufficient guarantees to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the processing meets the requirements of the GDPR.
The contract must be binding on the processor, setting out the responsibilities of the processor in the context of the processing.

In cases where the processor has establishments in more than one Member State, the contract must specify the place of the processor's central administration in the Union or, if the processor has no central administration, the establishment where the main processing activities take place.
The contract may be an individual contract or a standard contractual clause, which can be adopted by the Commission or a supervisory authority.
The controller and its representative must maintain a record of processing activities, as required by Article 30(1).
The record must contain the name and contact details of the controller, joint controller, representative, and data protection officer.
The purposes of the processing, categories of data subjects and personal data, and categories of recipients must be included in the record.
Personal data must be stored for no longer than necessary for the purposes of processing, unless it is stored for archiving purposes or scientific research.
The record must also include information on the categories of recipients, including those in third countries or international organisations.
The record must be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing.

Ensure an appropriate level of security, including confidentiality, taking into account the state of the art and the costs of implementation in relation to the risks and the nature of the personal data to be protected, as per Article 16 of the GDPR.
Implement technical and organisational measures to ensure the principle of data minimisation, as required by Article 263 of the GDPR.

Conduct a systematic assessment of the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, including an assessment of the necessity and proportionality of the processing operations, as per Article 35 of the GDPR.
Implement safeguards, security measures, and mechanisms to address the risks, including measures to ensure the protection of personal data and demonstrate compliance with the GDPR.
Ensure that personal data is pseudonymised when necessary, as required by Article 263 of the GDPR.
Implement measures to ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of personal data, as required by the GDPR.
The controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach.
The notification must be made to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55.
The notification must be accompanied by reasons for the delay if it is not made within 72 hours.
The processor must notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach.
The notification may result in an intervention of the supervisory authority in accordance with its tasks and powers laid down in the Regulation.
The supervisory authority may facilitate the submission of complaints referred to in point (f) of paragraph 1 by measures such as a complaint submission form.
A personal data breach must be communicated to the affected individuals without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it.
The communication should be made as soon as reasonably feasible and in close cooperation with the supervisory authority, respecting guidance provided by it or by other relevant authorities.

The need to mitigate an immediate risk of damage may call for prompt communication with data subjects, whereas the need to implement appropriate measures against continuing or similar personal data breaches may justify more time for communication.

The controller shall notify the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
The processor shall notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach.
The notification to the supervisory authority should be accompanied by reasons for the delay if it is not made within 72 hours.

The new video surveillance feature may require a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) if it is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, particularly because it prevents data subjects from exercising a right or using a service or contract.
A DPIA is required for monitoring publicly accessible areas on a large scale, especially when using optic-electronic devices.

The processing of personal data should not be considered to be on a large scale if it concerns personal data from patients or clients by an individual physician, other health care professional, or lawyer.
A data protection impact assessment is required for processing operations that use new technologies and are likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
The controller shall seek the advice of the data protection officer, where designated, when carrying out a data protection impact assessment.

A data protection impact assessment is required for certain activities, such as monitoring relevant developments, adopting standard contractual clauses, and establishing and maintaining a list of requirements for DPIA.
A data protection officer must be designated on the basis of professional qualities, expert knowledge of data protection law and practices, and the ability to fulfill tasks referred to in Article 39.
The data protection officer may be a staff member of the controller or processor, or fulfill tasks on the basis of a service contract.
The controller or processor shall publish the contact details of the data protection officer and communicate them to the supervisory authority.
The data protection officer shall be bound by secrecy or confidentiality concerning the performance of their tasks, in accordance with Union or Member State law.
The data protection officer shall directly report to the highest management level of the controller or processor.

The controller or processor shall ensure that the data protection officer does not receive any instructions regarding the exercise of their tasks, and that they are not dismissed or penalized for performing their tasks.
Transfers to third countries and international organisations can only take place in full compliance with the GDPR.
The conditions for transferring personal data to a third country must be complied with by the controller or processor.
The GDPR allows for international agreements between the EU and third countries to regulate the transfer of personal data, including appropriate safeguards for data subjects.
The scale of the collection and sharing of personal data has increased significantly, bringing new challenges for the protection of personal data.

The GDPR provides a framework for transfers of personal data to third countries, including decisions pursuant to Article 45, which are without prejudice to transfers of personal data to specific sectors within a third country.

The GDPR also provides a chapter on transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations, which includes provisions for cooperation and exchange of personal data between public and private actors.
Standard contractual clauses are used to regulate data transfers between controllers and processors, including intra-group data transfers, as per Article 28(8) of the GDPR.

Binding corporate rules are used to ensure the protection of personal data within a group of undertakings or enterprises, and standard contractual clauses can be used to implement these rules, as per Article 47 of the GDPR.

The European Commission has the power to adopt standard contractual clauses for intra-group data transfers, including those for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, as per Article 263(40) of the GDPR.

Standard contractual clauses can be used to regulate the tasks of data protection officers and other persons or entities in charge of monitoring compliance with binding corporate rules, as per Article 47(h) of the GDPR.

Binding corporate rules can be used to ensure the verification of compliance with these rules, and standard contractual clauses can be used to implement this verification process, as per Article 47(j) of the GDPR.

The GDPR allows for the use of standard contractual clauses and binding corporate rules to regulate intra-group data transfers, and the Commission may lay down these clauses for the matters referred to in Article 28(3) and 4 of the GDPR.
The maximum administrative fine for infringing the GDPR is up to 10,000,000 EUR or 2% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.
Infringements of certain provisions, such as those related to certification bodies, may be subject to administrative fines up to 10,000,000 EUR.
The GDPR requires Member States to lay down rules on penalties applicable to infringements, including administrative fines, which shall be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive.
The GDPR also requires the establishment of guidelines for supervisory authorities concerning the application of measures, including administrative fines, to ensure consistency and proportionality.
The GDPR encourages the drawing-up of codes of conduct and the establishment of data protection certification mechanisms and data protection seals and marks to promote compliance and risk assessment.
The GDPR requires the review of practical application of guidelines, recommendations, and best practices to ensure their effectiveness in promoting compliance and risk assessment.
The principle of data minimization requires that personal data be collected and processed only to the extent necessary for the specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes.
Data minimization aims to limit the amount of personal data collected and processed, ensuring that only the necessary data is used for the intended purposes.
The principle of data minimization is closely related to the concept of purpose limitation, which requires that personal data be processed in a manner that is compatible with the initial purposes.

In certain cases, such as for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes, data minimization may not be possible, and alternative measures must be taken to protect the data subject's rights and freedoms.

The principle of data minimization is essential for ensuring that personal data is not collected or processed in a way that is excessive or unnecessary, thereby protecting the data subject's rights and freedoms.

The principle of data minimization is also closely linked to the concept of transparency, which requires that data controllers provide clear and concise information about the purposes of data collection and processing.

Personal data may be stored for longer periods insofar as the personal data will be processed solely for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes in accordance with Article 89(1).

The personal data should be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes for which they are processed, including ensuring that the period for which the personal data are stored is limited to a strict minimum.
The storage periods and the applicable safeguards taking into account the nature, scope and purposes of the processing or categories of processing should be determined.

The processing of personal data for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes should be subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of the data subject pursuant to this Regulation.

The further processing of personal data for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes is to be carried out when the controller has assessed the feasibility to fulfil those purposes by processing data which do not permit or no longer permit the identification of data subjects.
The right of data subjects to be informed about the restriction, unless that may be prejudicial to the purpose of the restriction, should be considered.

A company established outside the EU that offers goods to people in the EU may be subject to GDPR regulations, as the GDPR applies to any company processing the personal data of EU residents, regardless of its location.
The GDPR allows for the imposition of administrative fines for infringements, and each supervisory authority has the power to impose these fines, as stated in Article 263 of the GDPR.

The GDPR also provides for the concept of "binding corporate rules" (BCRs), which are legally binding and apply to and are enforced by every member concerned of the group of undertakings, or group of enterprises engaged in a joint economic activity.

The GDPR aims to contribute to the accomplishment of an area of freedom, security and justice, and to economic and social progress, and seeks to harmonize the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons in respect of processing activities.

The GDPR does not explicitly address the issue of non-EU e-commerce stores, but the concept of BCRs may be relevant in this context, as it provides a framework for groups of undertakings to establish rules for processing personal data.
The GDPR's scope is not limited to EU companies, but rather applies to any company processing the personal data of EU residents, regardless of its location or nationality.
Data protection by design and by default requires the implementation of safeguards to ensure compliance with data protection requirements and the rights of data subjects.

The measures envisaged to address risks, including safeguards, security measures, and mechanisms to ensure the protection of personal data, must be taken into account when assessing the impact of processing operations.

Data protection by design and by default must be implemented in accordance with the general principles relating to personal data processing, including purpose limitation, data minimization, limited storage periods, and data quality.

The controller and processor must ensure that data protection by design and by default is implemented in a way that respects the rights and legitimate interests of data subjects and other persons concerned.
The implementation of data protection by design and by default must be subject to regular reviews and assessments to ensure ongoing compliance with data protection requirements.
The data protection officer must be independent and not receive instructions that may conflict with their duties, and must be able to report directly to the highest management level.

When two organisations jointly determine the purposes and means of processing, they must ensure that the processing is lawful and necessary in the context of a contract or the intention to enter into a contract.
The processing should have a basis in Union or Member State law, including laws that determine the purpose of processing.
The joint determination of purposes and means of processing may be necessary for reasons of substantial public interest, on the basis of Union or Member State law.
The processing may be necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller.

The legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party, including the co-branded loyalty programme, must be balanced against the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject.
The joint processing must be subject to suitable and specific measures to safeguard the fundamental rights and the interests of the data subject.
A data subject can lodge a complaint about how their data is processed with a supervisory authority, as per Article 16 of the GDPR.
The GDPR requires that controllers provide data subjects with information about the rights they have, including the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority.

The GDPR also requires that controllers provide information about the measures they take to ensure the security of processing, as well as the notification of personal data breaches to supervisory authorities.

In addition, the GDPR provides data subjects with the right to exercise their rights, including the right to lodge a complaint with the competent supervisory authority and before the competent courts of the Member States.

The GDPR also requires that controllers provide information about the application of the general data protection principles, including the right to lodge a complaint with the competent supervisory authority.
Furthermore, the GDPR provides data subjects with the right to obtain redress and, where appropriate, compensation for a breach of the binding corporate rules.
A person may not be able to claim compensation for damage caused by an infringement, as the GDPR does not explicitly provide for compensation in all cases.
In cases where a minor infringement is committed, a reprimand may be issued instead of a fine, and the GDPR does not provide for compensation in such cases.

The GDPR provides for the right to compensation and liability for damages caused by an infringement, and any person who has suffered material or non-material damage as a result of an infringement shall have the right to receive compensation from the controller or processor.

The GDPR also provides for the liability of controllers and processors, stating that a processor shall be liable for the damage caused by processing only where it has not complied with obligations of the Regulation specifically directed to processors or where it has acted outside or contrary to lawful instructions of the controller.
The GDPR does not provide for compensation for damage caused by an infringement in all cases, and the right to compensation is subject to certain conditions and limitations.

In cases where multiple controllers or processors are involved in the same processing, each controller or processor shall be held liable for the entire damage in order to ensure effective compensation of the data subject.
The data subject has the right to obtain from the controller without undue delay the rectification of inaccurate personal data concerning him or her, as stated in Article 16 of the GDPR.
The data subject shall have the right to have incomplete personal data completed, including by means of providing a supplementary statement, taking into account the purposes of the processing.

The controller must take reasonable steps, including technical measures, to inform other controllers that process the personal data of the data subject's request for erasure, as stated in Article 17 of the GDPR.

The data subject has the right to request from the controller rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning the data subject, as stated in Article 15 of the GDPR.

The data subject's right to rectification of inaccurate personal data is a fundamental right that must be respected by the controller, and the controller must take every reasonable step to ensure that personal data that are inaccurate are erased or rectified without delay.

The GDPR requires that the controller provide the data subject with information about the rectification or erasure of personal data, including the existence of the right to request such action, as stated in Article 15 of the GDPR.
A data subject can obtain restriction of processing if the processing is not allowed under specific cases set out in the GDPR, taking into account Member States law.
The restriction of processing means the marking of stored personal data with the aim of limiting their processing in the future.

The GDPR allows for restriction of processing in certain cases, such as when the processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller.

The right to restriction of processing is subject to certain conditions, including the need to ensure that the processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller.
The GDPR also requires that the storage periods and applicable safeguards be taken into account when determining whether to restrict processing.
The data subject has the right to be informed about the restriction, unless that may be prejudicial to the purpose of the restriction.
Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences is allowed under Article 10 of the GDPR, which specifically permits the processing of such data.
The GDPR also requires a data protection impact assessment for processing personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences, particularly when it is processed on a large scale.

The GDPR's provisions on processing personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences are separate from those on personal data referred to in Article 9(1), which covers more general categories of personal data.

The GDPR's rules on processing personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences are subject to specific requirements and exemptions, such as those related to the independence of the judiciary.

The GDPR's supervisory authorities may establish lists of processing operations that are subject to a data protection impact assessment, including those related to personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences.

The GDPR's provisions on processing personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences may be subject to specific exemptions or limitations, such as those related to the activities of forensic laboratories or anti-money laundering.

The legitimate interests of a controller can provide a legal basis for processing personal data, as long as the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject are not overriding, taking into consideration the reasonable expectations of data subjects based on their relationship with the controller.

The GDPR requires that controllers provide data subjects with information necessary to ensure fair and transparent processing, including the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or a third party, where processing is based on point (f) of Article 6(1).

Processing is lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the conditions in Article 6(1) is met, including where the processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject.

The GDPR also requires that controllers provide data subjects with the right to request access to and rectification or erasure of personal data, or restriction of processing concerning the data subject, and to object to processing.

In the context of fraud detection, legitimate interests may be a relevant legal basis for processing personal data, particularly where there is a relevant and appropriate relationship between the data subject and the controller.

However, the GDPR also emphasizes the importance of transparency and fairness in processing, and requires that controllers provide data subjects with meaningful information about the logic involved in automated decision-making, including profiling.
Consent from a lawful guardian is required for the processing of personal data of children, as stated in Section 6 (part 25) of the DPDP Act, 2023.
The Data Fiduciary shall not undertake tracking or behavioural monitoring of children or targeted advertising directed at children, as per Section 6 (part 25) of the DPDP Act, 2023.

The provisions of Section 6 (part 25) of the DPDP Act, 2023, shall not be applicable to processing of personal data of a child by certain classes of Data Fiduciaries or for certain purposes, subject to certain conditions.
The DPDP Act, 2023, prescribes specific conditions for obtaining verifiable consent from Data Principals, including children, as per Section 8 (part 25).
The Significant Data Fiduciary shall undertake certain measures, including Data Protection Impact Assessment, for processing personal data of children, as per Section 10.

The DPDP Act, 2023, defines "data" as a representation of information, facts, concepts, opinions or instructions in a manner suitable for communication, interpretation or processing by human beings or by automated means.
The Consent Manager must give a notice to the Data Principal before seeking consent, as stated in Section 6 (part 10) of the DPDP Act, 2023.
The notice given by the Data Fiduciary to the Data Principal must inform her of the purpose of processing her personal data, as per Section 8 (part 23) of the DPDP Act, 2023.
The notice must also inform the Data Principal of the rights and obligations of the Consent Manager, as per Section 8 (part 23) of the DPDP Act, 2023.
The Data Principal must exhaust the opportunity of redressing her grievance under Section 7 (part 4) of the DPDP Act, 2023 before approaching the Board.
The notice given by the Data Fiduciary to the Data Principal must be in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder, as stated in Section 10 of the DPDP Act, 2023.
The purpose of processing personal data must be a lawful purpose, as defined in Section 2 of the DPDP Act, 2023.
Valid consent must be given by the Data Principal, and the Data Fiduciary shall inform the Data Principal under sub-section (1) of section 5.
The Data Principal has the right to withdraw her consent at any time, with the ease of doing so being comparable to the ease with which such consent was given.
The Data Fiduciary or Consent Manager shall respond to any grievances referred to in sub-section (1) within such period as may be prescribed.
The Consent Manager acts as a single point of contact to enable a Data Principal to give, manage, review and withdraw her consent through an accessible, transparent and interoperable platform.
The Data Principal shall exhaust the opportunity of redressing her grievance under this section before approaching the Board.

The consequences of the withdrawal of consent shall be borne by the Data Principal, and such withdrawal shall not affect the legality of processing of the personal data based on consent before its withdrawal.

A Data Principal has the right to withdraw their consent at any time, with the ease of doing so being comparable to the ease with which such consent was given, as per Section 6 (part 7) of the DPDP Act, 2023.

The consequences of withdrawing consent shall be borne by the Data Principal, and such withdrawal shall not affect the legality of processing of the personal data based on consent before its withdrawal, as per Section 6 (part 7) of the DPDP Act, 2023.
A Data Principal can withdraw consent through an accessible, transparent, and interoperable platform, facilitated by a Consent Manager, as defined in Section 7 (part 4) of the DPDP Act, 2023.

The Data Fiduciary or Consent Manager shall respond to any grievances referred to in Section 7 (part 4) of the DPDP Act, 2023, within a prescribed period, as per Section 7 (part 2) of the DPDP Act, 2023.
In the event of death or incapacity of the Data Principal, the rights of the Data Principal shall be exercised by another individual, as per Section 7 (part 3) of the DPDP Act, 2023.
The Board may issue directions to a person concerned, as per Section 8 (part 2) of the DPDP Act, 2023, after giving the person an opportunity of being heard and recording reasons in writing.

A Consent Manager is a person registered with the Board who acts as a single point of contact to enable a Data Principal to give, manage, review, and withdraw her consent through an accessible, transparent, and interoperable platform.
The Consent Manager is accountable to the Data Principal and shall act on her behalf in such manner and subject to such obligations as may be prescribed.
The Consent Manager shall be registered with the Board in such manner and subject to such technical, operational, financial, and other conditions as may be prescribed.

The Consent Manager is responsible for ensuring that the Data Principal's consent is given, managed, reviewed, and withdrawn in accordance with the provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
In case of a breach of any condition of registration of a Consent Manager, the Board may inquire into such breach and impose penalty as provided in the Act.
The Consent Manager shall be bound to comply with directions issued by the Board for the effective discharge of its functions under the provisions of the Act.
Personal data can be processed without consent for the purpose of preventing or detecting offences or cyber incidents, as per Section 7 (part 2) of the DPDP Act.
Personal data can be processed without consent for the purpose of prosecution or punishment of offences, as per Section 7 (part 2) of the DPDP Act.

Personal data can be processed without consent for the purpose of erasure of personal data for the processing of which the individual has previously given consent, as per Section 7 (part 2) of the DPDP Act.
Personal data can be processed without consent for the purpose of correcting, completing, or updating personal data, as per Section 7 (part 2) of the DPDP Act.
Personal data can be processed without consent for the purpose of fulfilling a contractual obligation, as implied by Section 6 (part 8) of the DPDP Act.
Personal data can be processed without consent for a lawful purpose, which means any purpose that is not expressly forbidden by law, as per Section 2 (2) of the DPDP Act.
